item.title: The Re-Foundation of Radar Meteorology
item.description: arXiv:2611.08659v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Since the early development of radar meteorology in the 1940s, rainfall retrieval has traditionally relied on empirical scaling relationships between radar variables and rainfall rate. Here, we revisit the premise that horizontal and differential reflectivity sufficiently constrain the rainfall rate despite the variability of the underlying drop size distribution. Motivated by evidences that this variability requires at least three degrees of freedom, we develop a nonparametric statistical retrieval algorithm that considers different combinations of drop count and distribution shape compatible with the same radar observations. The method separates the contributions of drop count and distribution shape. It then empirically estimates how the shape factors for rainfall rate and horizontal reflectivity, as well as differential reflectivity, vary with the mean and skewness of the drop diameter distribution. These relationships identify compatible combinations of drop count and shape, from which rainfall rates are calculated and their median returned as the estimate. Neither a prescribed analytical drop size distribution nor a scaling rainfall estimator or explicit classification of precipitation regimes is required. We evaluate the method using a worldwide database (149 disdrometer datasets from 76 locations), with radar observables calculated from measured drop spectra. In cross-dataset validation, the method achieves lower median dispersion of relative retrieval errors across all 16 combinations of training and validation instrument types with respect two benchmark methods consisting of the traditional scaling law relationship, and a direct nonparametric fit. These findings motivate a reassessment of the foundations of radar rainfall retrieval by incorporating the range of rainfall rates compatible with radar observation.
item.dc:creator: Massimiliano Ignaccolo, Carlo De Michele

item.title: Half-precision inference of AI weather prediction models: negligible loss of skill at a fraction of the cost
item.description: arXiv:2611.09573v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AI weather prediction models are released with 32-bit (fp32) weights and run in fp32 by default, although current GPUs compute much faster in 16-bit formats. We run five publicly available models -- Aurora, Pangu-Weather, FourCastNet, SFNO and FastNet -- on a single 16 GB GPU from 52 initial dates in 2024, in fp32 and with their networks in half precision (fp16), and verify the forecasts against ERA5. The physical state must stay in fp32: converting the whole model rounds it in physical units, which in fp16 overflows and in bf16 discards meaningful information. With the state, its normalisation and denormalisation in fp32, running the network in fp16 changes the global RMSE by at most 1.4%, and by about 0.5% or less for four of the five models, equivalent to less than one hour of lead time up to day 8 and at most two hours at day 10. The differences show no systematic pattern by region, scale or for tropical and extratropical storms, apart from a small tropical penalty in FourCastNet, and fp16 leaves the CRPS, spread and calibration of Aurora's ensemble almost unchanged. No value overflowed fp16's numeric range (+/-65,504); the largest stay 38 to 544 times below it. A 10-day forecast in fp16 is 1.3-3.5 times faster than in fp32 and uses 1.4-3.7 times less energy. Sensitivity experiments show that rules of thumb from other applications of reduced precision carry over only partly: the first and last layers dominate for some models but not for others, and no type of layer is sensitive on its own. For running AI weather models on a single GPU, fp16 with the state in fp32 is practically lossless at a fraction of the cost. bf16, often preferred for its wider range, is as fast but less accurate than fp16 for every model, and simple 8-bit quantisation costs far more skill.
item.dc:creator: Stefan Siegert

item.title: RainFlow: Flow Matching for Infrared-Only Quantitative Precipitation Estimation
item.description: arXiv:2611.09663v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Geostationary infrared imagers observe precipitating systems every 10 to 15 minutes over large areas, but they sense cloud tops rather than the rain beneath. Their brightness temperatures constrain surface rain only weakly, so retrievals trained by regression return a smooth estimate that misses heavy rain and carries no measure of uncertainty. We treat infrared-only retrieval as conditional generation and introduce RainFlow, a flow-matching model that generates ensembles of rain fields from MSG/SEVIRI infrared observations, in a direct and a residual variant. Evaluated against radar over metropolitan France for a full year, the generated members are realistic rain fields, with the observed dry areas, heavy rain and spatial structure, and the ensemble mean is as accurate as a deterministic baseline. Used as probabilities, the ensembles locate heavy rain at scales where the baseline has no skill, and their spread captures most of the retrieval error, with only slight underdispersion. Trained with a time-sampling density that favours the noise end of the generative trajectory, the two variants reach similar skill. The direct variant depends strongly on this choice of density, whereas the residual variant is nearly insensitive to it. Evaluating the generated rain as a function of brightness temperature shows that the ensembles reproduce how rain depends on it over most of the range. It also isolates the remaining gap, an underestimate of both the amount and the variability of rain under the coldest cloud tops, which scores computed over all pixels do not reveal.
item.dc:creator: Matthieu Meignin (LATMOS), C\'ecile Mallet (LATMOS), Nicolas Viltard (LATMOS)

item.title: TitanMPAS - a new global and regional Titan atmospheric circulation model. Part I: Global model results
item.description: arXiv:2611.08700v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We developed TitanMPAS, a new Titan global and regional climate model, to simulate atmospheric dynamics and methane cycles. It integrates the non-hydrostatic MPAS dynamical core and TitanWRF physics parameterizations, with corrections to relax the thin-atmosphere assumptions on the gravity and curvature terms. TitanMPAS improves upon TitanWRF by incorporating a better moist convection parameterization and the observed surface properties. Long-term simulations ($>$100 Titan years) with a high resolution of $1^\circ$ and the realistic topography show that TitanMPAS is able to produce the stratospheric superrotation with typical equatorial wind speed over $\rm 120\,ms^{-1}$ and the maximum zonal wind speed exceeding $\rm 170\,ms^{-1}$ . Besides the good match of temperature profiles to the Cassini CIRS observations, the simulated wind, temperature and methane abundance in the troposphere match well with Huygens probe in-situ measurements. TitanMPAS also captures the major features of seasonal methane precipitation distribution patterns inferred from the observed cloud activities, as well as the vertical and latitudinal variations of methane abundance in the reanalysis of Cassini VIMS data. Resolution sensitivity studies show that higher resolution produces faster stratospheric superrotation, as well as stronger near-surface wind due to better resolved terrain variations. We further demonstrate that, despite the weak solar insolation, the near-surface temperature, pressure, wind magnitude and methane abundance all exhibit diurnal variations. Lastly, we show potential impacts of topography on methane transport and eddy momentum flux in both troposphere and stratosphere, which should be investigated in a future study.
item.dc:creator: Yuan Lian, Mark I. Richardson, Claire E. Newman, Martin A. Cordiner

item.title: Raytracing and quantifying the inferior mirage
item.description: arXiv:2611.09131v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Using custom raytracing code, we explore several features of the inferior mirage that are not widely discussed, such as the blurring in the mirage image, and what happens to the light in the direct image region that is replaced by the mirage image. The raytracing model also clarifies how to quantify the mirage, and we provide expressions to calculate the angular extent of the mirage under given thermal conditions and measurement geometry.
item.dc:creator: Nathan Hagen, Lucas Reyes Bentancor, Kakeru Tanaka, Norimasa Hanaya, Momo Shoda, Hiroki Maki, Takuma Ando, Keisaku Yoshizawa, Kayo Suzuki, Yume Yamada, Asana Kumakura

item.title: Reconciling advective upwelling with diapycnal downwelling: A transient kinematic perspective on Munk's conundrum
item.description: arXiv:2502.21006v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Bottom-intensified turbulent fluxes observed near the seafloor drive abyssal densification and diapycnal downwelling through their vertical divergence. This appears paradoxical under steady stratification because dense bottom waters continuously enter from Antarctic sources. Motivated by evolving Indo-Pacific stratification, we use idealized simulations to examine abyssal overturning under transient and steady-state conditions. Using a kinematic rather than thermodynamic water-mass-transformation approach, we diagnose advective overturning, isopycnal volume tendency, and diapycnal transport in two cooling experiments with different mixing intensities, one warming experiment, and one quasi-equilibrium experiment. Advective upwelling occurs in all four, whereas diagnosed diapycnal transport varies in direction. In Type-I cooling, the isopycnal volume tendency exceeds advective overturning in magnitude, yielding downward diapycnal transport; in Type-II cooling, advective overturning exceeds the isopycnal volume tendency, yielding upward diapycnal transport. The warming and quasi-equilibrium experiments also exhibit upward diapycnal transport. These relationships persist qualitatively in potential-temperature coordinates. Type-I cooling also spontaneously produces an observationally documented bottom-intensified buoyancy-flux profile with an e-folding scale comparable to previous estimates. Thus, cooling alone does not determine diapycnal transport direction; it depends kinematically on the relative strengths of advective overturning and isopycnal volume tendency. Within this idealized framework, the results provide a transient kinematic interpretation of the interior-downwelling conundrum: abyssal waters can rise through the basin interior while undergoing diapycnal downwelling, without requiring an upslope return pathway within the bottom boundary layer.
item.dc:creator: Lei Han

item.title: Sensitivity of the IceCube atmospheric muon rate to decadal trends in the effective atmospheric temperature
item.description: arXiv:2611.00918v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Decadal changes in the Antarctic stratosphere, generally associated with ozone recovery and shifts in polar circulation, are of broad geophysical interest. However, independent long-term measurements of the atmosphere above the Antarctic interior are scarce. We assess whether the atmospheric muon rate recorded by IceCube could constrain decadal changes in the effective atmospheric temperature, $T_\mathrm{eff}$, a weighted average of temperature through the atmosphere that is most sensitive to the stratosphere. Using public atmospheric reanalysis data and records of cosmic-ray, solar, and geomagnetic variability, we reproduce the measured seasonal response of the IceCube muon rate. We then test whether the same response applies to long-term temperature changes with a different vertical temperature profile. The limiting requirement is detector stability rather than counting statistics: an unmodeled muon rate drift of $1\%\,\mathrm{decade^{-1}}$ would mimic a temperature trend of $2.8\,\mathrm{K\,decade^{-1}}$. The long-term rate must therefore be stable to approximately $0.3\%\,\mathrm{decade^{-1}}$. Within this budget, snow accumulation contributions can be constrained. For a 14-year record, atmospheric variability gives a one-sided 95% CL statistical sensitivity of $1.6\,\mathrm{K\,decade^{-1}}$. Given this sensitivity, the $\sim0.9,\mathrm{K,decade^{-1}}$ cooling indicated by the 2011-2025 atmospheric records would be constrained at the 95% confidence level after approximately 22 years of measurement.
item.dc:creator: Tanvi Krishnan, Gabriela Barenboim, Carlos A. Arg\"uelles
